solution.summary: [Sample response – sample mode ignores what you typed.] Fix the board-level numbers first with a short, manual reconciliation, then build a single reporting data store in a second phase once metric definitions and owners are agreed.
steps: Agree on the 10–15 metrics the board relies on, with one definition each.
Name a client-side owner for each metric.
Reconcile those metrics manually for the next board pack.
Build a single reporting data store fed by the three systems.
Move the board pack onto the new data store and retire the manual process.

reasoning: Definitions come first because the three systems disagree mainly on what each metric means, not on the raw data.
Owners are named early so data quality doesn't slip again once the project team leaves.
A manual reconciliation is a stopgap that protects the fixed board deadline without waiting for new technology.
The data store comes second because building it before definitions are agreed would bake the inconsistencies into the new system.
Retiring the manual process at the end avoids running two versions of the truth.

questions.question: Why does the solution agree on metric definitions before building anything?
questions.answer: Because the systems mainly disagree on what each metric means; building first would carry those inconsistencies into the new system.
key_points: building first would bake in inconsistencies

questions.question: What is the manual reconciliation in step 3 protecting against?
questions.answer: Missing the fixed board deadline while the longer-term data store is still being built.

questions.question: Why name an owner for each metric?
questions.answer: So someone stays accountable for data quality after the project ends, preventing the problem from returning.

questions.question: Why does the last step retire the manual process?
questions.answer: To avoid two competing versions of the numbers once the data store is live.
